nodes.name: Fermat's Last Theorem
nodes.statement: Fermat's Last Theorem (FLT) is one of the most renowned results in the history of mathematics. Originally conjectured by Pierre de Fermat in 1637, the theorem asserts that there are no three positive integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ that can satisfy the equation $a^n + b^n = c^n$ for any integer value of $n$ greater than $2$.
assumptions: integer value of $n$ greater than $2$
conclusions: there are no three positive integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ that can satisfy the equation $a^n + b^n = c^n$

nodes.name: Monoid
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set.\\ Let $\circ: X\times X \to X$ be an internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{monoid} is a pair $\cc{M}:= (X, \circ)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\circ y)\circ z= x\circ (y\circ z) = x\circ y \circ z$ \item [\textbf{(N)}] $\exists e \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\circ e = e \circ x = x$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A set with an associative operation and an identity element.

nodes.name: Commutative Monoid
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set.\\ Let $\circ: X\times X \to X$ be an internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{commutative monoid} is a pair $\cc{M}_c:= (X, \circ)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\circ y)\circ z= x\circ (y\circ z) = x\circ y \circ z$ \item [\textbf{(N)}] $\exists e \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\circ e = e \circ x = x$ \item [\textbf{(C)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\circ y = y\circ x$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A monoid whose operation is commutative.

nodes.name: GCD Monoid
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set.\\ Let $\circ: X\times X \to X$ be an internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{gcd monoid} is a pair $\cc{M}_{\gcd}:= (X, \circ)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\circ y)\circ z= x\circ (y\circ z) = x\circ y \circ z$ \item [\textbf{(N)}] $\exists e \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\circ e = e \circ x = x$ \item [\textbf{(C)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\circ y = y\circ x$ \item [\textbf{(G)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ \exists d \in X : (d\divides x) \land (d\divides y) \land \left(\forall c \in X,\ c\divides x \land c\divides y \Rightarrow c\divides d\right)$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A commutative monoid in which any two elements have a greatest common divisor.

nodes.name: Group
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set.\\ Let $\circ: X\times X \to X$ be an internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{group} is a pair $\cc{G}:= (X, \circ)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\circ y)\circ z= x\circ (y\circ z) = x\circ y \circ z$ \item [\textbf{(N)}] $\exists e \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\circ e = e \circ x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists x'\in X: x\circ x' = x'\circ x = e$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A monoid in which every element has an inverse.

nodes.name: Commutative Group
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set.\\ Let $\circ: X\times X \to X$ be an internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{commutative group} is a pair $\cc{G}_c:= (X, \circ)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\circ y)\circ z= x\circ (y\circ z) = x\circ y \circ z$ \item [\textbf{(N)}] $\exists e \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\circ e = e \circ x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists x'\in X: x\circ x' = x'\circ x = e$ \item [\textbf{(C)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\circ y = y\circ x$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A group whose operation is commutative.

nodes.name: Semiring
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{semiring} is a triple $\cc{S}:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Commutative additive monoid and multiplicative monoid with two-sided distributivity.

nodes.name: Commutative Semiring
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{commutative semiring} is a triple $\cc{S}_c:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(C2)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\cdot y = y\cdot x$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Ring
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{ring} is a triple $\cc{R}:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I1)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Commutative Ring
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{commutative ring} is a triple $\cc{R}_c:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I1)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(C2)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\cdot y = y\cdot x$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Left Ideal
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a ring. \\\\ A \textit{left ideal} is a subset $I \subseteq X$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(SG)}] $(I, +)$ is a subgroup of $(X, +)$ \item [\textbf{(L)}] $\forall i\in I,\ \forall x\in X,\ x\cdot i\in I$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Additive subgroup closed under left multiplication by ring elements.

nodes.name: Right Ideal
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a ring. \\\\ A \textit{right ideal} is a subset $I \subseteq X$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(SG)}] $(I, +)$ is a subgroup of $(X, +)$ \item [\textbf{(R)}] $\forall i\in I,\ \forall x\in X,\ i\cdot x\in I$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Additive subgroup closed under right multiplication by ring elements.

nodes.name: Ideal
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a ring. \\\\ An \textit{ideal} or \textit{two-sided ideal} is a subset $I \subseteq X$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(SG)}] $(I, +)$ is a subgroup of $(X, +)$ \item [\textbf{(L)}] $\forall i\in I,\ \forall x\in X,\ x\cdot i\in I$ \item [\textbf{(R)}] $\forall i\in I,\ \forall x\in X,\ i\cdot x\in I$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Additive subgroup closed under left and right multiplication.

nodes.name: Domain
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{domain} is a triple $\cc{D}:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I1)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(Z2)}] $\forall x,y \in X,\ x\cdot y = 0 \Rightarrow x=0 \lor y=0$ \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Commutative Domain
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{commutative} or \textit{integral domain} is a triple $\cc{D}_c:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I1)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(C2)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\cdot y = y\cdot x$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(Z2)}] $\forall x,y \in X,\ x\cdot y = 0 \Rightarrow x=0 \lor y=0$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A commutative ring without zero divisors.

nodes.name: Field
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{field} is a triple $\bb{F}:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I1)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I2)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists x^{-1}\in X: x\cdot x^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot x = 1$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A ring in which every element has a multiplicative inverse (as written, including 0).

nodes.name: Commutative Field
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: X\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative internal composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \textit{commutative field} is a triple $\bb{F}_c:= (X, +, \cdot)$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A1)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C1)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N1)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I1)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(A2)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x\cdot y)\cdot z= x\cdot(y\cdot z) = x\cdot y\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(C2)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x\cdot y = y\cdot x$ \item [\textbf{(N2)}] $\exists 1 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x\cdot1 = 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I2)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists x^{-1}\in X: x\cdot x^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot x = 1$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ x\cdot(y+z)=x\cdot y+x\cdot z$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall x,y,z \in X,\ (x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Fundamental System of Field
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field endowed with a topology $\mathcal{T}$. \\ Let $I \subseteq \N$ be an index set. \\\\ A \textit{fundamental system} of $X$ is a collection \( \mathcal{U} = \{ U_i \}_{i \in I} \) of open sets in \( X \) such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $\forall i \in I,\ 0 \in U_i$. \item $\forall V \ni 0,\ \exists i \in I : U_i \subseteq V$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A family of open sets containing 0 that forms a neighbourhood base at 0.

nodes.name: Vector Space
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. \\ Let $(\K,+,\cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $+: X\times X \to X$ be an additive internal composition law on $X$. \\ Let $\cdot: \K\times X \to X$ be a multiplicative external composition law on $X$. \\\\ A \K-\textbf{vector space} or \K-\textbf{linear space} is a triple $\cc{V}:= (X, +, \cdot)_{\K}$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item [\textbf{(A)}] $\forall x,y,z\in X,\ (x+y)+z= x+(y+z) = x+y+z$ \item [\textbf{(C)}] $\forall x,y\in X,\ x+y = y+x$ \item [\textbf{(N)}] $\exists 0 \in X : \forall x \in X,\ x+0 = 0+x = x$ \item [\textbf{(I)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \exists (-x)\in X: x+(-x) = (-x)+x = 0$ \item [\textbf{(P)}] $\forall x \in X,\ \forall k,\ell \in \K,\ k\cdot_X(\ell\cdot_X x)= (k\cdot_{\K}\ell)\cdot_X x$ \item [\textbf{(U)}] $\exists 1 \in \K : \forall x \in X,\ 1\cdot x = x$ \item [\textbf{(D1)}] $\forall x,y \in X,\ \forall k\in \K,\ k\cdot(x+_Xy)=k\cdot x+_Xk\cdot y$ \item [\textbf{(D2)}] $\forall k,\ell \in \K,\ \forall x\in X,\ (k+_\K\ell)\cdot x=k\cdot x+_X\ell\cdot x$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: An abelian group with a compatible scalar multiplication by a field $\K$.

nodes.name: Notation $X$ for an algebraic structure
nodes.statement: From now on, we shall employ the notation $X$ in place of the more explicit $(X, +, \cdot)$ to denote a field, commutative ring, domain, or similar algebraic structures when the context unambiguously implies the operations involved.
nodes.statement_short: Write $X$ for a structure $(X,+,\cdot)$ when the operations are clear.

nodes.name: Field Extension
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $(Y, +, \cdot)$ be a field such that $Y \subseteq X$. \\\\ A \textit{field extension} is the pair $X/Y$ such that the operations of $Y$ are those of $X$ restricted to $Y$.

nodes.name: Degree of Field Extension
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $(Y, +, \cdot)$ be a field such that $Y \subseteq X$. \\ Let $X/Y$ be a field extension. \\\\ The \textit{degree} of $X/Y$, denoted as $[Y:X]$, is the dimension of $X$ as a vector space over $Y$.
nodes.genus: dimension of $X$ as a vector space over $Y$

nodes.name: Algebraic Field Extension
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $(Y, +, \cdot)$ be a field such that $Y \subseteq X$. \\\\ An \textit{algebraic field extension} is the field extension $X/Y$ such that its degree $[Y:X]$ is finite.

nodes.name: Extension Field
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $(Y, +, \cdot)$ be a field such that $Y \subseteq X$. \\ Let $X/Y$ be a field extension. \\\\ The field $X$ is said to be an \textit{extension field} of $Y$.

nodes.name: Subfield
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $(Y, +, \cdot)$ be a field such that $Y \subseteq X$. \\ Let $X/Y$ be a field extension. \\\\ The field $Y$ is said to be a \textit{subfield} of $X$.

nodes.name: Number Field
nodes.statement: Let $(X, +, \cdot)$ be a field. \\ Let $(\Q, +, \cdot)$ be the field of rational numbers such that $\Q \subseteq X$. \\ Let $X/\Q$ be an algebraic field extension. \\\\ The extension field $X$ is said to be a \textit{number field} or an \textit{algebraic number field}.

nodes.name: Root of Unity
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N_{+}$. \\\\ A \textit{$n$-th root of unity} is an element $\zeta \in \C$ such that $\zeta^n = 1$.

nodes.name: Primitive Root of Unity
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N_{+}$. \\\\ A \textit{primitive $n$-th root of unity} is an element $\zeta \in \C$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item $\zeta^n = 1$. \item $\forall k \in \N_{+},\ k < n \implies \zeta^k \neq 1$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Cyclotomic Polynomial
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N_{+}$. \\ Let $\zeta \in \C$ be a primitive $n$-th root of unity. \\\\ The \textit{$n$-th cyclotomic polynomial} is the unique monic polynomial with integer coefficients whose roots are the primitive $n$-th roots of unity: $$ \Phi_n(x) = \prod_{\substack{1 \leq k \leq n \\ \gcd(k, n) = 1}} \left( x - \zeta^k \right)$$
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi_n(x)=\prod_{\gcd(k,n)=1}(x-\zeta^k)$, the monic integer polynomial whose roots are the primitive $n$-th roots of unity.

nodes.name: Cyclotomic Extension Field
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N_{+}$. \\ Let $\zeta_n \in \C$ be a primitive $n$-th root of unity. \\ Let $X$ be a field. \\\\ The \textit{$n$-th cyclotomic extension field} or \textit{$n$-th cyclotomic field} is a field $X(\zeta_n)$ obtained by adjoining $\zeta_n$ to $X$.

nodes.name: zeta_sub_one_prime'
nodes.statement: Let $p \in \N$ be prime. \\\\ If $\zeta_p$ is a primitive $p$-th root of unity, then $\zeta_p - 1$ is prime.
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta_p-1$ is prime for a primitive $p$-th root of unity, $p$ prime.
assumptions: $p \in \N$ be prime
$\zeta_p$ is a primitive $p$-th root of unity

nodes.name: cube_of_castHom_ne_zero
nodes.statement: Let $\Z_9$ be the ring of integers modulo $9$. \\ Let $\Z_3$ be the ring of integers modulo $3$. \\ Let $n \in \Z_9$. \\ Let $\phi : \Z_9 \to \Z_3$ be the canonical ring homomorphism. \\ Let $\phi(n) \neq 0$. \\ \\ Then $n^3=1 \lor n^3=8$.
nodes.statement_short: In $\Z_9$, an element nonzero mod 3 has cube $1$ or $8$.
assumptions: $\Z_9$ be the ring of integers modulo $9$
$\Z_3$ be the ring of integers modulo $3$
$n \in \Z_9$

nodes.statement: Let $\cc{F}$ be the fundamental system of $K$. \\ By properties of cyclotomic fields, we know that $\rank{K} = 0$ (see \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Embeddings.html#NumberField.InfinitePlace.card_eq_nrRealPlaces_add_nrComplexPlaces}{this lemma}, \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Embeddings.html#IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.nrRealPlaces_eq_zero}{this lemma} and \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Embeddings.html#IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.nrComplexPlaces_eq_totient_div_two}{this lemma} which have already been formalised and included in Mathlib). nodes.name: not_exists_int_three_dvd_sub
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $m \in \Z$. \\\\ Then $3 \notdivides \eta - m$.

$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$

nodes.name: Proof of not_exists_int_three_dvd_sub
nodes.statement: By properties of cyclotomic fields, we know that $\set{1,\eta}$ is an integral power basis of $\cc{O}_K$ (see \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Rat.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.integralPowerBasis'}{this lemma}, \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Rat.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.power_basis_int'_dim}{this lemma} and \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Rat.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.integralPowerBasis'_gen}{this lemma} which have already been formalised and included in Mathlib).\\ For every $\xi \in \cc{O}_K$, we define $\pi_1(\xi)$ and $\pi_2(\xi)$ to be the first and second coordinates of $\xi$ with respect to the basis $\set{1,\eta} \in \cc{O}_K$, i.e. $$\xi = \pi_1(\xi) + \pi_2(\xi)\eta.$$ By contradiction we assume that $$\exists m \in \Z \text{ such that } 3 \divides \eta - m,$$ which implies that $$\exists x \in \cc{O}_K \text{ such that } \eta - m = 3 x.$$ By linearity of $\pi_2$, $$\pi_2(\eta) = \pi_2(3x + m) = 3\pi_2(x) + \pi_2(m).$$ Since $\pi_2(\eta) = 1$ and $\pi_2(m) = 0$, then we have that $3 \divides 1$, which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction via the second coordinate in the integral basis $\{1,\eta\}$.

nodes.name: $\{1,\eta\}$ is an integral power basis
nodes.statement: By properties of cyclotomic fields, we know that $\set{1,\eta}$ is an integral power basis of $\cc{O}_K$ (see \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Rat.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.integralPowerBasis'}{this lemma}, \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Rat.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.power_basis_int'_dim}{this lemma} and \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/FLT3/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Rat.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.integralPowerBasis'_gen}{this lemma} which have already been formalised and included in Mathlib).

nodes.name: Define coordinate maps $\pi_1,\pi_2$
nodes.statement: For every $\xi \in \cc{O}_K$, we define $\pi_1(\xi)$ and $\pi_2(\xi)$ to be the first and second coordinates of $\xi$ with respect to the basis $\set{1,\eta} \in \cc{O}_K$, i.e. $$\xi = \pi_1(\xi) + \pi_2(\xi)\eta.$$

nodes.name: Assume $\eta-m=3x$
nodes.statement: By contradiction we assume that $$\exists m \in \Z \text{ such that } 3 \divides \eta - m,$$ which implies that $$\exists x \in \cc{O}_K \text{ such that } \eta - m = 3 x.$$

nodes.name: Apply $\pi_2$
nodes.statement: By linearity of $\pi_2$, $$\pi_2(\eta) = \pi_2(3x + m) = 3\pi_2(x) + \pi_2(m).$$

nodes.name: Get $3\mid1$, contradiction
nodes.statement: Since $\pi_2(\eta) = 1$ and $\pi_2(m) = 0$, then we have that $3 \divides 1$, which is a contradiction.

nodes.name: Proof of lambda_sq
nodes.statement: By definition we have that $\lambda = \eta -1$, which implies that $$\lambda^2 = (\eta - 1)^2 = \eta^2 - 2\eta + 1.$$ Since $\eta$ corresponds to a root of the equation $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$, then $\eta^2 = -1 - \eta$. Substituting back, we can conclude that $$\lambda^2 = (-1 - \eta) - 2\eta + 1 = -3\eta.$$

nodes.name: Expand $\lambda^2$
nodes.statement: By definition we have that $\lambda = \eta -1$, which implies that $$\lambda^2 = (\eta - 1)^2 = \eta^2 - 2\eta + 1.$$

nodes.name: Use $\eta^2+\eta+1=0$
nodes.statement: Since $\eta$ corresponds to a root of the equation $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$, then $\eta^2 = -1 - \eta$.

nodes.name: Substitute to get $-3\eta$
nodes.statement: Substituting back, we can conclude that $$\lambda^2 = (-1 - \eta) - 2\eta + 1 = -3\eta.$$

By \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq}, we have that $-3\eta = \lambda^2 \divides u - m$, which implies that $3 \divides u - m$.\ By \Cref{thm:mem}, we know that $u \in \set{1, -1, \eta, -\eta, \eta^2, -\eta^2}$. \ We proceed by analysing each case:  egin{itemize} \item Case $u = 1 \lor u = -1$. eq \eta$. \item Case $u = -\eta$.\ Since $3 \divides u - m$, we have that $3 \divides - \eta - m$, then by properties of divisibility $3 \divides \eta + m$, which contradicts \Cref{thm:not_exists_int_three_dvd_sub} forcing us to conclude that $u 
eq -\eta$. \item Case $u = \eta^2$.\ Since $3 \divides u - m$, we have that $3 \divides \eta^2 - m$, which contradicts \Cref{thm:not_exists_int_three_dvd_sub} since $\eta^2$ is a third root of unity (see \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/Mathlib/RingTheory/RootsOfUnity/Basic.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.pow_of_coprime}{Mathlib}), forcing us to conclude that $u 
eq \eta^2$. \item Case $u = -\eta^2$.\ Since $3 \divides u - m$, we have that $3 \divides - \eta^2 - m$, then by properties of divisibility $3 \divides \eta^2 + m$, which contradicts \Cref{thm:not_exists_int_three_dvd_sub} since $\eta^2$ is a third root of unity (see \href{https://pitmonticone.github.io/FLT3/docs/Mathlib/RingTheory/RootsOfUnity/Basic.html#IsPrimitiveRoot.pow_of_coprime}{Mathlib}), forcing us to conclude that $u 
eq -\eta^2$. \end{itemize} Therefore, $u = 1 \lor u = -1$.

nodes.name: Proof of univ_quot
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:card_quot}, the cardinality of $\cc{O}_K / I$ is $3$, so it suffices to prove that $1,-1$ and $0$ are distinct.\\ We proceed by contradiction analysing each case: \begin{itemize} \item Case $1 = -1$. By basic algebraic properties, $1 = -1$ implies that $2 = 0$, which contradicts \Cref{lmm:two_ne_zero} forcing us to conclude that $1 \neq -1$. \item Case $1 = 0$. nodes.name: Exclude $-1=0$

nodes.name: Proof of lambda_dvd_mul_sub_one_mul_sub_eta_add_one
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:dvd_or_dvd_sub_one_or_dvd_add_one}, we have that $$(\lambda \divides x) \lor (\lambda \divides x-1) \lor (\lambda \divides x+1).$$ We proceed by analysing each case: \begin{itemize} \item Case $\lambda \divides x$. \\ By properties of divisibility, we have that $\lambda \divides x(x - 1)(x - (\eta + 1))$. \item Case $\lambda \divides x-1$. \\ By properties of divisibility, we have that $\lambda \divides x(x - 1)(x - (\eta + 1))$. \item Case $\lambda \divides x+1$.\\ By properties of divisibility, it suffices to prove that $$\lambda \divides x - (\eta + 1) = x + 1 - (\eta - 1 + 3).$$ By definition of $\lambda$, we have that $$x + 1 - (\eta - 1 + 3) = x + 1 - (\lambda + 3).$$ By properties of divisibility and \Cref{lmm:lambda_dvd_three}, we can deduce that $\lambda \divides \lambda + 3$.\\ Therefore, by properties of divisibility, we can conclude that $$\lambda \divides x(x - 1)(x - (\eta + 1)).$$ \end{itemize}

nodes.name: First factor
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda \divides x$. \\ By properties of divisibility, we have that $\lambda \divides x(x - 1)(x - (\eta + 1))$.

nodes.name: Second factor
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda \divides x-1$. \\ By properties of divisibility, we have that $\lambda \divides x(x - 1)(x - (\eta + 1))$.

nodes.name: Third factor via $\lambda\mid3$
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda \divides x+1$.\\ By properties of divisibility, it suffices to prove that $$\lambda \divides x - (\eta + 1) = x + 1 - (\eta - 1 + 3).$$ By definition of $\lambda$, we have that $$x + 1 - (\eta - 1 + 3) = x + 1 - (\lambda + 3).$$ By properties of divisibility and \Cref{lmm:lambda_dvd_three}, we can deduce that $\lambda \divides \lambda + 3$.\\ Therefore, by properties of divisibility, we can conclude that $$\lambda \divides x(x - 1)(x - (\eta + 1)).$$

nodes.statement: Let $\lambda \divides x - 1$, which is equivalent to say that $$\exists y\in \cc{O}_K \text{ such that } x - 1 = \lambda y.$$ By ring properties and \Cref{lmm:cube_sub_one}, we have that $$x^3 - 1 = \lambda^3 (y (y - 1) (y - (\eta + 1))).$$ By properties of divisibility and \Cref{lmm:lambda_dvd_mul_sub_one_mul_sub_eta_add_one}, we can conclude that $$\lambda^ 4 \divides x^3 - 1.$$

nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $x$ mod $\lambda$ using the two preceding lemmas.

nodes.name: Split on $x$ mod $\lambda$
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:dvd_or_dvd_sub_one_or_dvd_add_one}, we have that $$(\lambda \divides x) \lor (\lambda \divides x-1) \lor (\lambda \divides x+1).$$ We proceed by analysing each case:

nodes.name: Contradictory case
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda \divides x$. From trivially contradictory hypotheses we can conclude that $$(\lambda^4 \divides x^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides x^3 + 1).$$

nodes.name: Apply the $x-1$ lemma
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda \divides x-1$. By \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_of_dvd_sub_one}, we have that $\lambda^ 4 \divides x^3 - 1$, which implies that $$(\lambda^4 \divides x^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides x^3 + 1).$$

nodes.name: Apply the $x+1$ lemma
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda \divides x+1$. By \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_add_one_of_dvd_add_one}, we have that $\lambda^ 4 \divides x^3 + 1$, which implies that $$(\lambda^4 \divides x^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides x^3 + 1).$$

nodes.name: cube_of_not_dvd
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N$. \\ Let $\left[n \right] \in \Z_9$. \\ Let $3 \notdivides n$. \\ \\ Then $\left[n \right]^3 = 1 \lor \left[n \right]^3 = 8$.
assumptions: $n \in \N$
$\left[n \right] \in \Z_9$
$3 \notdivides n$
nodes.label: lmm:cube_of_not_dvd

nodes.name: Proof of cube_of_not_dvd
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:cube_of_castHom_ne_zero}, we can conclude that $\left[n \right]^3 = 1 \lor \left[n \right]^3 = 8$.

nodes.name: Fermat's Last Theorem for 3: Case 1
nodes.statement: Let $a, b, c \in \N$. \\ Let $3 \notdivides abc$. \\\\ Then $a ^ 3 + b ^ 3 \neq c ^ 3$.
assumptions: $a, b, c \in \N$
$3 \notdivides abc$
nodes.label: thm:fermatLastTheoremThree_case_1

nodes.name: Proof of Fermat's Last Theorem for 3: Case 1
nodes.statement:
By hypothesis we know that $3 
otdivides abc$, which implies that $3 
otdivides a$, $3 
otdivides b$ and $3 
otdivides c$. \ By repeatedly applying \Cref{lmm:cube_of_not_dvd} for each case, we can conclude that $$a ^ 3 + b ^ 3 
eq c ^ 3.$$
nodes.statement_short: Cubes mod 9 of numbers prime to 3 are $\pm1$, so $a^3+b^3\equiv c^3$ is impossible.

nodes.name: three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b
nodes.statement: Let $a, b, c \in \N$. \\ Let $3 \divides a$ and $3 \divides b$. \\ Let $a ^ 3 + b ^ 3 = c ^ 3$. \\\\ Then $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)$.
assumptions: $a, b, c \in \N$
$3 \divides a$ and $3 \divides b$
nodes.label: lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b

nodes.name: Proof of three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b
nodes.statement: By hypothesis we have that $3 \divides a^3 + b^3 = c^3$, which implies that $3 \divides c$, from which we can conclude that $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)$.

nodes.name: three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c
nodes.statement: Let $a, b, c \in \N$. \\ Let $3 \divides a$ and $3 \divides c$. \\ Let $a ^ 3 + b ^ 3 = c ^ 3$. \\\\ Then $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)$.
assumptions: $a, b, c \in \N$
$3 \divides a$ and $3 \divides c$
nodes.label: lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c

nodes.name: Proof of three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c
nodes.statement: By hypothesis we have that $3 \divides c^3 - a^3 = b^3$, which implies that $3 \divides b$, from which we can conclude that $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)$.

nodes.name: three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c
nodes.statement: Let $a, b, c \in \N$. \\ Let $3 \divides b$ and $3 \divides c$. \\ Let $a ^ 3 + b ^ 3 = c ^ 3$. \\\\ Then $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)$.
assumptions: $a, b, c \in \N$
$3 \divides b$ and $3 \divides c$
nodes.label: lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c

nodes.name: Proof of three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c
nodes.statement: By hypothesis we have that $3 \divides c^3 - b^3 = a^3$, which implies that $3 \divides a$, from which we can conclude that $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)$.

nodes.name: fermatLastTheoremThree_of_three_dvd_only_c
nodes.statement:
To prove \Cref{thm:fermatLastTheoremThree}, it suffices to prove that $$ orall a, b, c \in \Z, 	ext{ if } c 
eq 0 	ext{ and } 3 
otdivides a 	ext{ and } 3 
otdivides b 	ext{ and } 3 \divides c 	ext{ and } \gcd(a,b)=1, 	ext{ then } a^3 + b^3 
eq c^3.$$ Equivalently, $$ orall a, b, c \in \Z, 	ext{ if } c 
eq 0 	ext{ and } 3 
otdivides a 	ext{ and } 3 
otdivides b 	ext{ and } 3 \divides c 	ext{ and } \gcd(a,b)=1, 	ext{ then } a^3 + b^3 
eq c^3$$ implies \Cref{thm:fermatLastTheoremThree}.
nodes.statement_short:
FLT3 reduces to coprime $a,b$ with $3
mid a$, $3
mid b$, $3\mid c
eq0$.
conclusions:
it suffices to prove that $$ orall a, b, c \in \Z, 	ext{ if } c 
eq 0 	ext{ and } 3 
otdivides a 	ext{ and } 3 
otdivides b 	ext{ and } 3 \divides c 	ext{ and } \gcd(a,b)=1, 	ext{ then } a^3 + b^3 
eq c^3.$$
nodes.label: thm:fermatLastTheoremThree_of_three_dvd_only_c

nodes.name: Proof of fermatLastTheoremThree_of_three_dvd_only_c
nodes.statement:
By contradiction we assume that $$\exists a,b,c \in \N \smallsetminus \set{0} 	ext{ such that } a^3 + b^3 = c^3.$$ By \Cref{lmm:fermatLastTheoremWith_of_fermatLastTheoremWith_coprime} we can assume that $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. \ By \Cref{thm:fermatLastTheoremThree_case_1} we can assume that $3 \divides a b c$, from which it follows that $$(3 \divides a) \lor (3 \divides b) \lor (3 \divides c).$$ We proceed by analysing each case:  egin{itemize} \item Case $3 \divides a$. \ Let $a'=-c$, $b'=b$, $c'=-a$, then $3 \divides c'$ and $$(a'
eq 0) \land (b'
eq 0) \land (c' 
eq 0).$$ Then $3 
otdivides a'$ since otherwise by \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c} we would have that $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)=1$ which is absurd. \ Analogously, by \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b} we have that $3 
otdivides b'$.\ By contradiction we assume that $\gcd(a',b') 
eq 1$ which, by basic divisibility properties, implies that there is a prime $p$ such that $p \divides a'$ and $p \divides b'$. It follows that $p \divides b'^3 + a'^3 = b^3 - c^3 = -a^3$, which implies that $p \divides a$.\ Therefore $p \divides \gcd(a,b,c)=1$ which is absurd. \ Moreover, we have that $a'^3 + b'^3 = -c^3 + b^3 = -a^3 = c'^3$ that contradicts our hypothesis. \item Case $3 \divides b$. \ Let $a'=a$, $b'=-c$, $c'=-b$.\ The rest of the proof is analogous to the first case using \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b} and \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c}. \item Case $3 \divides c$. Let $a'=a$, $b'=b$, $c'=c$.\ The rest of the proof is analogous to the first case using \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c} and \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c}. \end{itemize} Therefore, we can conclude that $a^3 + b^3 
eq c^3$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: assume coprime, use Case 1, then permute signs so that 3 divides only $c'$. The key step checks coprimality of the permuted pair.

nodes.name: Assume a solution, reduce to $\gcd=1$ and $3\mid abc$
nodes.statement: By contradiction we assume that $$\exists a,b,c \in \N \smallsetminus \set{0} \text{ such that } a^3 + b^3 = c^3.$$ By \Cref{lmm:fermatLastTheoremWith_of_fermatLastTheoremWith_coprime} we can assume that $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. \\ By \Cref{thm:fermatLastTheoremThree_case_1} we can assume that $3 \divides a b c$, from which it follows that $$(3 \divides a) \lor (3 \divides b) \lor (3 \divides c).$$ We proceed by analysing each case:
nodes.statement_short: Assume a solution, reduce to $\gcd=1$ and $3\mid abc$

nodes.name: Case $3\mid a$: swap to $(-c,b,-a)$
nodes.statement:
Case $3 \divides a$. \ Let $a'=-c$, $b'=b$, $c'=-a$, then $3 \divides c'$ and $$(a'
eq 0) \land (b'
eq 0) \land (c' 
eq 0).$$ Then $3 
otdivides a'$ since otherwise by \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c} we would have that $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)=1$ which is absurd. \ Analogously, by \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b} we have that $3 
otdivides b'$.\ By contradiction we assume that $\gcd(a',b') 
eq 1$ which, by basic divisibility properties, implies that there is a prime $p$ such that $p \divides a'$ and $p \divides b'$. It follows that $p \divides b'^3 + a'^3 = b^3 - c^3 = -a^3$, which implies that $p \divides a$.\ Therefore $p \divides \gcd(a,b,c)=1$ which is absurd. \ Moreover, we have that $a'^3 + b'^3 = -c^3 + b^3 = -a^3 = c'^3$ that contradicts our hypothesis.

nodes.name: Define $a',b',c'$
nodes.statement:
Let $a'=-c$, $b'=b$, $c'=-a$, then $3 \divides c'$ and $$(a'
eq 0) \land (b'
eq 0) \land (c' 
eq 0).$$

nodes.name: $3\nmid a'$
nodes.statement: Then $3 \notdivides a'$ since otherwise by \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c} we would have that $3 \divides \gcd(a,b,c)=1$ which is absurd.

nodes.name: $3\nmid b'$
nodes.statement: Analogously, by \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b} we have that $3 \notdivides b'$.

nodes.name: $\gcd(a',b')=1$
nodes.statement: By contradiction we assume that $\gcd(a',b') \neq 1$ which, by basic divisibility properties, implies that there is a prime $p$ such that $p \divides a'$ and $p \divides b'$. It follows that $p \divides b'^3 + a'^3 = b^3 - c^3 = -a^3$, which implies that $p \divides a$.\\ Therefore $p \divides \gcd(a,b,c)=1$ which is absurd.

nodes.name: New triple is a forbidden solution
nodes.statement: Moreover, we have that $a'^3 + b'^3 = -c^3 + b^3 = -a^3 = c'^3$ that contradicts our hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: New triple is a forbidden solution

nodes.name: Case $3\mid b$: analogous
nodes.statement: Case $3 \divides b$. \\ Let $a'=a$, $b'=-c$, $c'=-b$.\\ The rest of the proof is analogous to the first case using \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_b} and \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c}.

nodes.name: Case $3\mid c$: analogous
nodes.statement: Case $3 \divides c$. Let $a'=a$, $b'=b$, $c'=c$.\\ The rest of the proof is analogous to the first case using \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_a_of_dvd_c} and \Cref{lmm:three_dvd_gcd_of_dvd_b_of_dvd_c}.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can conclude that $a^3 + b^3 \neq c^3$.

nodes.name: Solution'
nodes.statement:
Let $a, b, c \in \cc{O}_K$ such that $c 
eq 0$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$.\ Let $\lambda 
otdivides a$, $\lambda 
otdivides b$ and $\lambda \divides c$. \\ A 	extit{solution'} is a tuple $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ satisfying the equation $a^3 + b^3 = u c^3.$
nodes.label: def:Solution1

nodes.name: Solution
nodes.statement:
Let $a, b, c \in \cc{O}_K$ such that $c 
eq 0$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$.\ Let $\lambda 
otdivides a$, $\lambda 
otdivides b$, $\lambda \divides c$ and $\lambda^2 \divides a+b$. \\ A 	extit{solution} is a tuple $S=(a, b, c, u)$ satisfying the equation $a^3 + b^3 = u c^3$.
nodes.label: def:Solution

nodes.name: Multiplicity of Solution'
nodes.statement: Let $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$. \\\\ The \textit{multiplicity} of $S'$ is the largest $n \in \N$ such that $\lambda^n \divides c$.
nodes.statement_short: The multiplicity of a solution' is the largest $n$ with $\lambda^n\mid c$.
nodes.label: def:Solution1_Multiplicity

nodes.name: Multiplicity of Solution
nodes.statement: Let $S=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution$. \\\\ The \textit{multiplicity} of $S$ is the largest $n \in \N$ such that $\lambda^n \divides c$.
nodes.statement_short: The multiplicity of a solution is the largest $n$ with $\lambda^n\mid c$.
nodes.label: def:Solution_Multiplicity

nodes.name: Minimal Solution
nodes.statement: Let $S=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution$. \\\\ We say that $S$ is \textit{minimal} if for all solutions $S_1=(a_1,b_1,c_1,u_1)$, the multiplicity of $S$ is less than or equal to the $multiplicity$ of $S_1$.
nodes.statement_short: A solution is minimal if its multiplicity is at most that of every solution.
nodes.label: def:Solution_Minimal

nodes.name: multiplicity_lambda_c_finite
nodes.statement: Let $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$. \\\\ Then the multiplicity of $S'$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: The multiplicity of a solution' is finite.
assumptions: $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$
nodes.label: lmm:multiplicity_lambda_c_finite

nodes.name: Proof of multiplicity_lambda_c_finite
nodes.statement: It directly follows from \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_unit}.

nodes.name: exists_minimal
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$. \\\\ Then there is a minimal solution $S_1$.
nodes.statement_short: If a solution exists, a minimal solution exists.
assumptions: $S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$
nodes.label: lmm:exists_minimal

nodes.name: Proof of exists_minimal
nodes.statement: Straightforward since $n \in \N$ and $\N$ is well-ordered.

nodes.name: a_cube_b_cube_same_congr
nodes.statement: Let $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$. \\\\ Then $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$ or $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: For a solution', $a^3$ and $b^3$ are $\pm1$ mod $\lambda^4$ with opposite signs.
assumptions: $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$
nodes.label: lmm:a_cube_b_cube_same_congr

nodes.name: Proof of a_cube_b_cube_same_congr
nodes.statement: Since $\lambda \notdivides a$, then $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \lor \lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1$ by \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd}. Since $\lambda \notdivides b$, then $\lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1 \lor \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$ by \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd}. We proceed by analysing each case: \begin{itemize} \item Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1$. Since $\lambda \divides c$ we have that $\lambda \divides c^3-(a^3-1)-(b^3-1) = 2$, which is absurd by \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_two}. \item Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$. Since $\lambda \divides c$ we have that $\lambda \divides (a^3-1)+(b^3-1)-c^3 = 2$, which is absurd by \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_two}. \item Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$. Trivial. \item Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1$. Trivial. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two $\pm1$ congruences; equal signs force $\lambda\mid2$.

nodes.name: Each of $a^3,b^3$ is $\pm1$ mod $\lambda^4$
nodes.statement: Since $\lambda \notdivides a$, then $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \lor \lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1$ by \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd}. Since $\lambda \notdivides b$, then $\lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1 \lor \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$ by \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd}. We proceed by analysing each case:

nodes.name: Both $+1$: $\lambda\mid2$
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1$. Since $\lambda \divides c$ we have that $\lambda \divides c^3-(a^3-1)-(b^3-1) = 2$, which is absurd by \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_two}.

nodes.name: Both $-1$: $\lambda\mid2$
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$. Since $\lambda \divides c$ we have that $\lambda \divides (a^3-1)+(b^3-1)-c^3 = 2$, which is absurd by \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_two}.

nodes.name: Mixed signs: done
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 - 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 + 1$. Trivial. \item Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1$. Trivial. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Mixed signs: done
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^4 \divides a^3 + 1 \land \lambda^4 \divides b^3 - 1$. Trivial. \end{itemize}

assumptions: $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$

nodes.name: Proof of lambda_pow_four_dvd_c_cube

nodes.statement_short: Use the congruences of $a^3,b^3$ and compute.

assumptions: $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$
nodes.label: lmm:lambda_pow_two_dvd_c

nodes.name: Proof of lambda_pow_two_dvd_c

nodes.name: cube_add_cube_eq_mul
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$.\\\\ Then $a^3 + b^3 = (a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b)$.
assumptions: $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field
$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$
nodes.label: lmm:cube_add_cube_eq_mul

nodes.name: Proof of cube_add_cube_eq_mul
nodes.statement: Straightforward calculation using \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one} and \Cref{lmm:toInteger_eval_cyclo}.

nodes.name: lambda_sq_dvd_or_dvd_or_dvd
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$. \\ Let $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$.\\\\ Then $(\lambda^2 \divides a + b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b)$.
assumptions: $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field
$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$
$S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$
conclusions: $(\lambda^2 \divides a + b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b)$
nodes.label: lmm:lambda_sq_dvd_or_dvd_or_dvd

nodes.name: Proof of lambda_sq_dvd_or_dvd_or_dvd
nodes.statement:
By contradiction we assume that $$(\lambda^2 
otdivides a + b) \land (\lambda^2 
otdivides a + \eta b) \land (\lambda^2 
otdivides a + \eta^2 b).$$ Then, by definition, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $a + b$, in $a + \eta b$ and in $a + \eta^2 b$ is less than $2$. By properties of divisibility, \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_two_dvd_c} and \Cref{lmm:cube_add_cube_eq_mul}, we have that $$\lambda^6 \divides u c^3 = a^3 + b^3 = (a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b).$$ Then, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $(a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b)$ is greater than or equal to $6$. \ By \Cref{lmm:lambda_prime} $\lambda$ is prime, so we have that the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $(a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b)$ is the sum of the multiplicities of $\lambda$ in $a + b$, in $a + \eta b$ and in $a + \eta^2 b$, which is less than $6$. This is a contradiction that forces us to conclude that $$(\lambda^2 \divides a + b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b).$$
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction by counting $\lambda$-adic valuations: the three factors have valuation $<2$ each, but the product has $\geq6$.

nodes.name: Assume each factor has valuation $<2$
nodes.statement:
By contradiction we assume that $$(\lambda^2 
otdivides a + b) \land (\lambda^2 
otdivides a + \eta b) \land (\lambda^2 
otdivides a + \eta^2 b).$$ Then, by definition, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $a + b$, in $a + \eta b$ and in $a + \eta^2 b$ is less than $2$.

nodes.name: $\lambda^6$ divides the product
nodes.statement: By properties of divisibility, \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_two_dvd_c} and \Cref{lmm:cube_add_cube_eq_mul}, we have that $$\lambda^6 \divides u c^3 = a^3 + b^3 = (a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b).$$ Then, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $(a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b)$ is greater than or equal to $6$.

nodes.name: Valuation is additive: sum $<6$
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:lambda_prime} $\lambda$ is prime, so we have that the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $(a + b) (a + \eta b) (a + \eta^2 b)$ is the sum of the multiplicities of $\lambda$ in $a + b$, in $a + \eta b$ and in $a + \eta^2 b$, which is less than $6$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: This is a contradiction that forces us to conclude that $$(\lambda^2 \divides a + b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b).$$

nodes.name: ex_dvd_a_add_b
nodes.statement: Let $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$.\\\\ Then $\exists a_1,b_1 \in \cc{O}_k$ such that $S_1=(a_1,b_1,c,u)$ is a $solution$.
nodes.statement_short: A solution' can be turned into a solution by replacing $b$ with $\eta^k b$.
assumptions: $S'=(a, b, c, u)$ be a $solution'$
nodes.label: lmm:ex_dvd_a_add_b

nodes.name: Proof of ex_dvd_a_add_b
nodes.statement:
By \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_dvd_or_dvd_or_dvd}, we have that $$(\lambda^2 \divides a + b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b).$$ We proceed by analysing each case:  egin{itemize} \item Case $\lambda^2 \divides a + b$. Trivial using $a_1=a$ and $b_1=b$. \item Case $\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b$. Let $a_1=a$ and $b_1=\eta b$. \ By \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, we have that $a^3 + (\eta b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 = u c^3$.\ By properties of coprimes and \Cref{lmm:eta_isUnit}, we have that $\gcd(a,b)=1$ implies that $\gcd(a,\eta b)=1$.\ Since $a_1=a$, we already know that $\lambda 
otdivides a = a_1$.\ By contradiction we assume that $\lambda \divides b_1 = \eta b$, which, by \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, it implies that $\lambda \divides \eta^2 \eta b = b$ that contradicts our assumption, forcing us to conclude that $\lambda 
otdivides b_1$. \item Case $\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b$. Let $a_1=a$ and $b_1=\eta^2 b$. \ By \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, we have that $a^3 + (\eta^2 b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 = u c^3$.\ By properties of coprimes and \Cref{lmm:eta_isUnit}, we have that $\gcd(a,b)=1$ implies that $\gcd(a,\eta^2 b)=1$.\ Since $a_1=a$, we already know that $\lambda 
otdivides a = a_1$.\ By contradiction we assume that $\lambda \divides b_1 = \eta^2 b$, which, by \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, it implies that $\lambda \divides \eta \eta^2 b = b$ that contradicts our assumption, forcing us to conclude that $\lambda 
otdivides b_1$. \end{itemize} Therefore, we can conclude that $\exists a_1,b_1 \in \cc{O}_k$ such that $S_1=(a_1,b_1,c,u)$ is a $solution$.

nodes.name: Split on which factor $\lambda^2$ divides
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_dvd_or_dvd_or_dvd}, we have that $$(\lambda^2 \divides a + b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b) \lor (\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b).$$ We proceed by analysing each case:

nodes.name: Keep $(a,b)$
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^2 \divides a + b$. Trivial using $a_1=a$ and $b_1=b$.

nodes.name: Use $b_1=\eta b$
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta b$. Let $a_1=a$ and $b_1=\eta b$. \\ By \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, we have that $a^3 + (\eta b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 = u c^3$.\\ By properties of coprimes and \Cref{lmm:eta_isUnit}, we have that $\gcd(a,b)=1$ implies that $\gcd(a,\eta b)=1$.\\ Since $a_1=a$, we already know that $\lambda \notdivides a = a_1$.\\ By contradiction we assume that $\lambda \divides b_1 = \eta b$, which, by \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, it implies that $\lambda \divides \eta^2 \eta b = b$ that contradicts our assumption, forcing us to conclude that $\lambda \notdivides b_1$.

nodes.name: Use $b_1=\eta^2 b$
nodes.statement: Case $\lambda^2 \divides a + \eta^2 b$. Let $a_1=a$ and $b_1=\eta^2 b$. \\ By \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, we have that $a^3 + (\eta^2 b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 = u c^3$.\\ By properties of coprimes and \Cref{lmm:eta_isUnit}, we have that $\gcd(a,b)=1$ implies that $\gcd(a,\eta^2 b)=1$.\\ Since $a_1=a$, we already know that $\lambda \notdivides a = a_1$.\\ By contradiction we assume that $\lambda \divides b_1 = \eta^2 b$, which, by \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, it implies that $\lambda \divides \eta \eta^2 b = b$ that contradicts our assumption, forcing us to conclude that $\lambda \notdivides b_1$.

nodes.name: A solution exists
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can conclude that $\exists a_1,b_1 \in \cc{O}_k$ such that $S_1=(a_1,b_1,c,u)$ is a $solution$.

nodes.name: exists_Solution_of_Solution1

nodes.name: Proof of z_eq_unit_mul_cube
nodes.statement: By the properties of PIDs, it suffices to prove that there exists a $k\in \cc{O}_K$ such that $zk$ is a cube and $\gcd(z,k)=1$. Let $k = xyu^{-1}$, then $zk = z x y u^{-1} = w^3$ by \Cref{lmm:x_mul_y_mul_z_eq_u_w_pow_three}. Moreover, since $\gcd(x,z)=1$ by \Cref{lmm:coprime_x_z} and $\gcd(y,z)=1$ by \Cref{lmm:coprime_y_z}, then $\gcd(z,xy)=1$, which implies that $\gcd(z,k)=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of coprime_Y_Z
nodes.statement:
Since $Z 
eq 0$ by \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_Z}, by the properties of PIDs it suffices to prove that $ orall p \in \cc{O}_K$ if $p$ is prime and $p \divides Y$, then $p 
otdivides Z$. Let $p \in \cc{O}_K$ be prime and suppose by contradiction that $p \divides Y$ and $p \divides Z$ which implies that $p \divides u_2 Y^3 = y$ and $p \divides \lambda u_3 Z^3 = z$. But this contradicts \Cref{lmm:coprime_y_z} forcing us to conclude that $p

nodes.name: formula1
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$. \\ Let $S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$.\\\\ Then $u_1 X^3 \lambda^{3n-2}+u_2 \eta Y^3 \lambda + u_3 \eta^2 Z^3 \lambda = 0$.
assumptions: $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field
$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$
$S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$
nodes.label: lmm:formula1

nodes.name: Proof of formula1
nodes.statement: Applying \Cref{def:Solution_u1_u2_u3_u4_u5_X_Y_Z}, \Cref{def:Solution_x_y_z_w}, \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one} and \Cref{lmm:toInteger_eval_cyclo}, we have \begin{align*} u_1 X^3 \lambda^{3n-2}+u_2 \eta Y^3 \lambda + u_3 \eta^2 Z^3 \lambda &= x \lambda^{3n-2} + \eta y \lambda + \eta^2 z \lambda \\ &= (a+b) + \eta (a+\eta b) + \eta^2 (a+\eta^2 b) \\ &= a (1 + \eta + \eta^2) + b (1 + \eta^4 + \eta^2) \\ &= (a+b)(1+\eta+\eta^2)\\ &= (a+b)0 = 0 \end{align*}

nodes.name: u₄_isUnit
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a $solution$.\\\\ Then $u_4$ is a unit.
assumptions: $S$ be a $solution$
nodes.label: lmm:u₄_isUnit

nodes.name: Proof of u₄_isUnit
nodes.statement: By \Cref{def:Solution_u1_u2_u3_u4_u5_X_Y_Z} $u_4 = \eta u_3 u_2^{-1}$, which is a product of units by \Cref{lmm:eta_isUnit}. Since the product of units is a unit (multiplicative closure), it follows that $u_4$ must also be a unit.

nodes.name: u₅_isUnit
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a $solution$.\\\\ Then $u_5$ is a unit.
assumptions: $S$ be a $solution$
nodes.label: lmm:u₅_isUnit

nodes.name: Proof of u₅_isUnit
nodes.statement: By \Cref{def:Solution_u1_u2_u3_u4_u5_X_Y_Z} $u_5 = -\eta^2 u_1 u_2^{-1}$, which is a product of units since $\eta^3 = 1$ by \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one} and $-\eta (-\eta^2) = \eta^3$. Since the product of units is a unit (multiplicative closure), it follows that $u_5$ must also be a unit.

nodes.name: formula2
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$. \\ Let $S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$.\\\\ Then $Y^3 + u_4 Z^3 = u_5 (\lambda^(n-1) X)^3$.
assumptions: $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field
$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$
$S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$
nodes.label: lmm:formula2

nodes.name: Proof of formula2
nodes.statement: Using \Cref{lmm:eta_isUnit}, \Cref{lmm:lambda_ne_zero}, it suffices to show that $$\lambda \eta u_2 (Y^3 + u_4 Z^3) = \lambda \eta u_2 u_5 (\lambda^(n-1) X)^3$$ which can be proved by simple calculations involving \Cref{lmm:toInteger_cube_eq_one}, \Cref{lmm:Solution_two_le_multiplicity} and \Cref{lmm:formula1}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $\lambda\eta u_2$ and use formula1.

nodes.name: lambda_sq_div_lambda_fourth

$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$
$S$ be a $solution$

nodes.name: lambda_sq_div_new_X_cubed
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$. \\ Let $S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$.\\\\ Then $\lambda^2 \divides u_5 (\lambda^{n - 1} X)^3$.
assumptions: $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field
$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$

nodes.name: Proof of lambda_sq_div_new_X_cubed
nodes.statement: Using \Cref{lmm:Solution_two_le_multiplicity}, we have that $\lambda^2 \divides \lambda^2 u_5 \lambda^{3n-5} X^3 = u_5 (\lambda^{n - 1} X)^3$.

nodes.name: by_kummer
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a $solution$.\\\\ Then $u_4 \in \set{-1,1} \subset \cc{O}_K$.
nodes.statement_short: $u_4=\pm1$, via the special case of Kummer's lemma.
assumptions: $S$ be a $solution$
nodes.label: lmm:by_kummer

nodes.name: Proof of by_kummer
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N$ be the multiplicity of the solution $S$.\\ By \Cref{lmm:eq_one_or_neg_one_of_unit_of_congruent}, it suffices to prove that $$\exists m \in \Z \text{ such that } \lambda^2 \divides u_4 - m.$$ By \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd} and \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_Y}, we have that $$(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 + 1).$$ By \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd} and \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_Z}, we have that $$(\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 + 1).$$ We proceed by analysing each case: \begin{itemize} \item Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 - 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 - 1)$. \\ Let $m=-1$ and consider the fact that $$u_4 - m = Y^3 + u_4 Z^3 - (Y^3 - 1) - u_4 (Z^3 - 1).$$ By \Cref{lmm:formula2}, we have that $$u_4 - m = u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3 - (Y^3 - 1) - u_4 (Z^3 - 1).$$ Since, by \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_div_new_X_cubed}, we know that $$\lambda^2 \divides u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3$$ and, by \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_div_lambda_fourth} and by assumption, we have that $$\lambda^2 \divides Y^3 - 1 \land \lambda^2 \divides Z^3 - 1,$$ Then, we can conclude that $$\lambda^2 \divides u_4 - m.$$ \item Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 - 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 + 1)$. \\ Let $m=1$ and proceed similarly to the first case. \item Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 + 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 - 1)$. \\ Let $m=1$ and proceed similarly to the first case. \item Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 + 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 + 1)$. \\ Let $m=-1$ and proceed similarly to the first case. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\lambda^2\mid u_4-m$ via the Kummer special case; case analysis on $Y^3,Z^3\equiv\pm1$ mod $\lambda^4$. The key step rewrites $u_4-m$ using formula2.

nodes.name: Reduce to a congruence; $Y^3,Z^3\equiv\pm1$ mod $\lambda^4$
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \N$ be the multiplicity of the solution $S$.\\ By \Cref{lmm:eq_one_or_neg_one_of_unit_of_congruent}, it suffices to prove that $$\exists m \in \Z \text{ such that } \lambda^2 \divides u_4 - m.$$ By \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd} and \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_Y}, we have that $$(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 + 1).$$ By \Cref{lmm:lambda_pow_four_dvd_cube_sub_one_or_add_one_of_lambda_not_dvd} and \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_Z}, we have that $$(\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 - 1) \lor (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 + 1).$$ We proceed by analysing each case:

nodes.name: Case $(+,+)$ with $m=-1$
nodes.statement: Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 - 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 - 1)$. \\ Let $m=-1$ and consider the fact that $$u_4 - m = Y^3 + u_4 Z^3 - (Y^3 - 1) - u_4 (Z^3 - 1).$$ By \Cref{lmm:formula2}, we have that $$u_4 - m = u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3 - (Y^3 - 1) - u_4 (Z^3 - 1).$$ Since, by \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_div_new_X_cubed}, we know that $$\lambda^2 \divides u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3$$ and, by \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_div_lambda_fourth} and by assumption, we have that $$\lambda^2 \divides Y^3 - 1 \land \lambda^2 \divides Z^3 - 1,$$ Then, we can conclude that $$\lambda^2 \divides u_4 - m.$$

nodes.name: Choose $m=-1$ and rewrite $u_4-m$
nodes.statement: Let $m=-1$ and consider the fact that $$u_4 - m = Y^3 + u_4 Z^3 - (Y^3 - 1) - u_4 (Z^3 - 1).$$

nodes.name: Substitute formula2
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:formula2}, we have that $$u_4 - m = u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3 - (Y^3 - 1) - u_4 (Z^3 - 1).$$

nodes.name: Each term divisible by $\lambda^2$
nodes.statement: Since, by \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_div_new_X_cubed}, we know that $$\lambda^2 \divides u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3$$ and, by \Cref{lmm:lambda_sq_div_lambda_fourth} and by assumption, we have that $$\lambda^2 \divides Y^3 - 1 \land \lambda^2 \divides Z^3 - 1,$$ Then, we can conclude that $$\lambda^2 \divides u_4 - m.$$

nodes.name: Case $(+,-)$ with $m=1$
nodes.statement: Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 - 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 + 1)$. \\ Let $m=1$ and proceed similarly to the first case.

nodes.name: Case $(-,+)$ with $m=1$
nodes.statement: Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 + 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 - 1)$. \\ Let $m=1$ and proceed similarly to the first case.

nodes.name: Case $(-,-)$ with $m=-1$
nodes.statement: Case $(\lambda^4 \divides Y^3 + 1) \land (\lambda^4 \divides Z^3 + 1)$. \\ Let $m=-1$ and proceed similarly to the first case.

nodes.name: final
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$. \\ Let $S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$.\\\\ Then $Y^3 + (u_4 Z)^3 = u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3$.
assumptions: $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field
$\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$
$\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$
$\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity
$\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$
$\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$
$S$ be a $solution$ with multiplicity $n$
nodes.label: lmm:final

nodes.name: Proof of final
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lmm:by_kummer}, we have that $u_4 \in \set{-1,1}$, which implies that $u_4^2 = 1$.\\ Therefore, by \Cref{lmm:formula2}, we can conclude that $$Y^3 + (u_4 Z)^3 = u_5 (\lambda^{n-1} X)^3.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Solution'_final_multiplicity
nodes.statement: Let $K = \Q(\zeta_3)$ be the third cyclotomic field. \\ Let $\cc{O}_K = \Z[\zeta_3]$ be the ring of integers of $K$. \\ Let $\cc{O}^\times_K$ be the group of units of $\cc{O}_K$. \\ Let $\zeta_3 \in K$ be any primitive third root of unity. \\ Let $\eta \in \cc{O}_K$ be the element corresponding to $\zeta_3 \in K$. \\ Let $\lambda \in \cc{O}_K$ be such that $\lambda = \eta -1$. \\ Let $(a',b',c',u') = S_f'$ be the final $solution'$, then $\lambda^{n-1} \divides \lambda^{n-1} X = c'$. By contradiction we assume that $\lambda^n \divides c'$ which implies that $\lambda \divides X$, that contradicts \Cref{lmm:lambda_not_dvd_X} forcing us to conclude that $\lambda^{n} \notdivides c'$. Then $S_f'$ has multiplicity $n-1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Generalised Fermat's Last Theorem for Exponent $3$
nodes.statement:
By contradiction we assume that there are $a, b, c \in \cc{O}_K$ and $u \in \cc{O}^	imes_K$ such that $c 
eq 0$, $\gcd(a,b)=1$, $\lambda 
otdivides a$, $\lambda 
otdivides b$, $\lambda \divides c$ and $a^3 + b^3 = u c^3$. Then $S'=(a,b,c,u)$ is a $solution'$, which implies that there is a $solution$ $S$ by \Cref{lmm:exists_Solution_of_Solution1}. Then, by \Cref{lmm:exists_minimal}, there is a minimal solution $S_0$ with multiplicity $n$. Hence, there is a $solution'$ $S_1'$ with multiplicity $m<n$ by \Cref{lmm:exists_Solution_multiplicity_lt}, which implies that there is a $solution$ $S_1$ with multiplicity $m$ by \Cref{lmm:exists_Solution_of_Solution1}. However, this contradicts the minimality of $S_0$ forcing us to conclude that $a^3 + b^3 
eq u c^3$.
nodes.statement_short: Infinite descent: a minimal solution yields one of smaller multiplicity.

nodes.name: Take a minimal solution
nodes.statement: Then, by \Cref{lmm:exists_minimal}, there is a minimal solution $S_0$ with multiplicity $n$.

nodes.name: Descend to smaller multiplicity
nodes.statement: Hence, there is a $solution'$ $S_1'$ with multiplicity $m<n$ by \Cref{lmm:exists_Solution_multiplicity_lt}, which implies that there is a $solution$ $S_1$ with multiplicity $m$ by \Cref{lmm:exists_Solution_of_Solution1}.

nodes.statement: However, this contradicts the minimality of $S_0$ forcing us to conclude that $a^3 + b^3 \neq u c^3$.
